body:
How education and the press encouraged organised political activity

During the 19th century, educated Indians increasingly formed organisations to discuss public affairs and demand changes in colonial administration.

Education supplied people with skills useful for writing petitions, examining policies, practising law and addressing meetings. Newspapers spread their arguments beyond individual towns. Political associations provided a more organised way to present shared demands.

Political mobilisation means bringing people together to support a political objective through activities such as meetings, petitions, campaigns and organised public discussion.

These processes worked together, but they were not identical. A school taught students, a newspaper circulated information, and a political association organised people around particular demands.

Important associations before the Congress

AssociationYearPlaceLeading figure or role
British Indian Association1851CalcuttaRepresented influential Indian interests through petitions
East India Association1866LondonDadabhai Naoroji; communicated Indian concerns to British audiences
Poona Sarvajanik Sabha1870PoonaAssociated with M. G. Ranade and other public figures
Indian Association1876CalcuttaSurendranath Banerjea and Anandamohan Bose
Madras Mahajana Sabha1884MadrasImportant regional political association
Bombay Presidency Association1885BombayPherozeshah Mehta, K. T. Telang and Badruddin Tyabji

Many associations were led by educated professionals, especially lawyers and other members of the urban middle class. Some earlier bodies represented relatively narrow social interests, while later organisations increasingly expressed claims on behalf of a wider Indian public.

Their methods included submitting petitions, holding meetings, collecting information and using newspapers to explain their demands.

Issues that encouraged wider political cooperation

The Vernacular Press Act, 1878

The attempt to restrict Indian-language newspapers strengthened criticism of colonial government policy. Political organisations treated press freedom as an important public concern because newspapers were among the main means available for discussing government actions.

The Ilbert Bill controversy, 1883

In 1883, the Ilbert Bill sought to address racial inequality in judicial authority by allowing qualified Indian judges and magistrates to try European British subjects in criminal cases.

Strong opposition from sections of the European community led to the weakening of the proposal. The controversy made racial discrimination in colonial institutions especially visible and encouraged Indian political cooperation.

Both disputes helped strengthen the belief that Indians required organisations capable of presenting common demands.

The Indian National Congress, 1885

The Indian National Congress held its first session in Bombay in December 1885, with 72 delegates attending.

W. C. Bonnerjee presided over the first session. A. O. Hume, a retired British official, played a role in bringing Indian political leaders together.

The Congress did not emerge independently of earlier public activity. Political associations had already developed methods of petitioning, conducting meetings and expressing demands in newspapers. They helped prepare the organisational foundations for an all-India forum.

The significance of the early political public sphere

Early nationalist leaders used articles, speeches and petitions to criticise colonial economic and administrative policies. Their demands included greater Indian participation in government, fairer access to public employment and protection of civil freedoms.

Newspapers made these demands more widely known. Reports from different regions helped people recognise that certain grievances were shared rather than purely local.

Nevertheless, early political organisations remained dominated by a relatively small educated section. The later development of broad mass participation in the national movement should not be projected backwards onto every association of the 19th century.

Putting the subtopic together

The history of colonial education and the press contains an important relationship. The British introduced educational policies partly for administrative and colonial purposes. Indians used educational institutions to obtain knowledge and professional skills. Print allowed social and political ideas to circulate, and associations helped organise responses to government policies.

The sequence was not automatic or uniform. Education remained unequal, newspapers could support opposing views, and political mobilisation also depended on economic grievances, racial discrimination and dissatisfaction with colonial rule.

The central distinction is that education developed skills and institutions, newspapers circulated ideas, and political associations organised collective demands. Together, they contributed to the growth of a more active Indian public sphere.

Prelims focus

  • East India Association: 1866, London, Dadabhai Naoroji.
  • Poona Sarvajanik Sabha: 1870.
  • Indian Association: 1876, associated with Surendranath Banerjea and Anandamohan Bose.
  • Ilbert Bill controversy: 1883, concerning racial inequality in judicial authority.
  • Indian National Congress: first session in Bombay, December 1885, attended by 72 delegates and presided over by W. C. Bonnerjee.
  • Trap: The Indian Association of 1876 and the Indian National Congress of 1885 were different organisations.

pictures.alt: Parallel education and press timelines feed into political associations, showing how skills, circulating ideas and organised demands strengthened participation.
pictures.caption: Education, newspapers and associations strengthened political participation through different functions.

title: Political Associations and Public Mobilisation: From Education and Newspapers to the Indian National Congress
